metadata.title: B1: Civic Reform Pressure
metadata.description: When trust falls far enough, citizens mobilize. Watergate produced the Ethics in Government Act of 1978. The 2008 financial crisis produced Dodd-Frank. Distrust, when channeled into civic activism, can pass reforms that reduce corruption and slowly rebuild trust.
metadata.author: US Government Intelligent Textbook

nodes.label: Trust In Government
nodes.description: The percentage of citizens who say they trust the federal government to do what is right most or all of the time.

nodes.label: Civic Activism
nodes.description: Voter turnout, protest movements, grassroots organizing, and demand for reform candidates.

nodes.label: Anti-Corruption Reforms
nodes.description: Laws like the Ethics in Government Act (1978), Inspector General reforms, campaign finance disclosure rules, and lobbying restrictions.

nodes.label: Political Corruption
nodes.description: Bribery, self-dealing, abuse of office, and other betrayals of the public trust.

edges.description: Falling trust mobilizes citizens — protest, organizing, and reform candidacies grow when people feel the system has gone wrong.
Sustained civic pressure forces Congress to pass anti-corruption legislation.

delay.description: Major reforms typically arrive 2–5 years after the scandal that prompted them.

edges.description: Disclosure rules, inspectors general, and ethics enforcement make corruption costlier and harder to hide.
Visible corruption — and the news coverage of it — drives trust down. Reducing corruption lets trust recover.

loops.label: B1: Civic Reform Pressure
loops.description: A self-correcting force: deep distrust eventually triggers the political will to reform — slowly restoring trust.
loops.behavior_pattern: Slow-acting brake. Works on a decade-long timescale and requires sustained activism.
